Traditional 3D computational models for direct oil-cooled electric vehicle (EV) batteries are often too computationally expensive for real-time integration into Battery Management Systems (BMS). To address this challenge, a novel Artificial Neural Network (ANN) framework is proposed to rapidly and accurately predict the coupled thermal and electrical performance of battery modules. The ANN is trained using high-fidelity experimental and simulation data collected under diverse operating conditions, including varying C-rates, oil flow rates, and inlet temperatures. The optimized model aims to achieve high predictive accuracy, with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) below a specified threshold for thermal metrics and an R² greater than 0.99 for electrical outputs such as terminal voltage and capacity. By significantly reducing inference time compared with traditional physics-based models, the proposed framework has the potential to enable real-time onboard predictions. This lightweight, data-driven approach could support advanced BMS functions, including proactive thermal regulation, thermal runaway risk mitigation, and improved commercial viability of direct oil-cooled EV battery systems.

Writing

Build a Professional Healthcare Process Mining Dashboard – CareFlow

Act as a senior UI/UX designer, healthcare data analyst, and full-stack dashboard developer. Design and build a modern, professional, interactive analytics dashboard for a project titled “CareFlow – Clinical Pathway Process Mining.”

1. Project objective

CareFlow analyzes synthetic Electronic Health Record (EHR) event-log data to understand patient journeys through a hospital. The dashboard should help users visualize clinical workflows, identify repeated activities, analyze patient journey durations, discover potential bottlenecks, and evaluate process performance using process mining and operational KPIs.

The dashboard must look like a professional healthcare analytics product suitable for a university project demonstration, internship evaluation, and portfolio presentation.

2. Visual design and theme

Use a clean, premium healthcare analytics design.

  • Primary colors: navy blue, medical teal, white, and light grey.

  • Background: very light grey or off-white.

  • Use a modern sans-serif font such as Inter.

  • Use rounded cards, subtle shadows, clean borders, and consistent spacing.

  • Use clear visual hierarchy and readable chart labels.

  • Include professional icons for patients, hospitals, activity tracking, time, and analytics.

  • Avoid excessive gradients, bright colors, clutter, and unnecessary animations.

  • Make the dashboard responsive for desktop, tablet, and mobile.

The overall appearance should resemble a professional hospital operations analytics platform.

3. Dashboard header

Display:

CareFlow
Clinical Pathway Process Mining & Healthcare Analytics

Include:

  • A healthcare analytics logo or simple medical workflow icon.

  • A short subtitle: “Transforming clinical event logs into actionable workflow insights.”

  • Date range filter.

  • Refresh button.

  • Data source indicator: “Synthetic EHR Event Log.”

  • Last updated timestamp, clearly identified as the dashboard refresh time.

4. Key Performance Indicator cards

Create visually attractive KPI cards at the top of the dashboard.

Include these metrics from the current dataset:

  • Total Patient Cases: 500

  • Total Recorded Events: 3,472

  • Clinical Activities: 7

  • Cases with Repeated Activities: 442

  • Cases with Repeated Triage: 126

  • Cases with Repeated Consultation-Related Activity: 410

Each card should include:

  • A relevant icon.

  • A large metric value.

  • A concise label.

  • A short explanatory tooltip.

Important: These are dataset-derived counts. Do not label repeated activities as confirmed inefficiencies.

5. Patient journey process visualization

Create a central section titled “Patient Journey – Process Flow.”

Visualize the clinical pathway using a clean process flow diagram:

Registration → Triage → Consultation → Lab Test / X-Ray → Treatment → Discharge

Requirements:

  • Display activities as connected nodes.

  • Show transition arrows between activities.

  • Display event frequency or transition frequency where available.

  • Highlight repeated activities and loopbacks.

  • Use different visual treatments for normal transitions and repeated transitions.

  • Allow users to explore individual activities and transitions.

Do not assume every patient follows exactly the same pathway. The diagram must reflect actual event-log data if process discovery results are available.

6. Activity analysis

Create an Activity Frequency Analysis section.

Include:

  • Bar chart showing the frequency of each clinical activity.

  • Activity distribution chart.

  • Repeated activity analysis.

  • A table showing activity name, event count, case count, and repeat count when those values are available.

Use the actual dataset to calculate chart values. Do not invent missing counts.

7. Patient journey duration analysis

Create a section titled “Patient Journey Duration.”

Include:

  • Average case duration.

  • Median case duration.

  • Minimum and maximum case duration.

  • Patient journey duration distribution.

  • Case duration comparison chart.

Calculate case duration using the difference between the first and last event timestamps for each case.

Clearly show the time unit and handle missing or invalid timestamps appropriately. Do not fabricate duration values.

8. Bottleneck and repeated activity analysis

Create a section titled “Potential Process Bottlenecks.”

Analyze:

  • Repeated triage activities.

  • Repeated consultation-related activities.

  • Long waiting intervals between consecutive events.

  • Frequently repeated activities.

  • Activities with unusually long delays.

Use neutral language such as “potential bottleneck,” “repeated activity,” and “long waiting interval.” Do not claim that a repeated activity proves poor clinical performance or unnecessary care.

Include charts and a ranked table of potential bottlenecks based on actual calculations.

9. Process performance and conformance

Create a section titled “Process Performance & Conformance.”

Include:

  • Observed patient pathways.

  • Common activity sequences.

  • Process variants.

  • Cases that follow a selected reference pathway, if one has been defined.

  • Deviations from the reference pathway, if conformance checking has been implemented.

If no reference model or conformance results are available, display a clear “Not yet calculated” or “Awaiting conformance analysis” status. Do not generate fake conformance scores.

10. Interactive filters

Add a professional filter panel with:

  • Case ID.

  • Activity name.

  • Date range.

  • Patient journey duration range.

  • Repeated activity status.

All charts, KPI cards, and tables should update based on the selected filters.

Include a reset filters option.

11. Detailed case explorer

Add a section titled “Patient Case Explorer.”

Provide a searchable table with:

  • Case ID.

  • First recorded activity.

  • Last recorded activity.

  • Total events.

  • Journey duration.

  • Repeated activity indicator.

When a user selects a case, show its chronological event timeline with activity names and timestamps.

Use synthetic case identifiers only. Do not display real patient-identifiable information.

12. Data and technical requirements

Use the cleaned event-log CSV as the primary data source.

Expected fields include:

  • Case ID

  • Activity

  • Timestamp

  • Event ID

Adapt to the actual column names in the supplied CSV.

Use the following data principles:

  • Calculate metrics dynamically from the uploaded dataset.

  • Do not hardcode analytical results except the verified initial dataset counts.

  • Handle missing values and duplicate events carefully.

  • Sort events chronologically within each case.

  • Keep all calculations consistent across dashboard sections.

  • Clearly distinguish calculated results from unavailable or pending analysis.

If backend integration is supported, structure the dashboard so that it can later connect to Python, PM4Py, BigQuery, and dbt.

13. Dashboard layout

Organize the dashboard in this order:

  1. Header and data source information.

  2. KPI overview cards.

  3. Patient journey process map.

  4. Activity frequency analysis.

  5. Patient journey duration analysis.

  6. Potential bottleneck analysis.

  7. Process performance and conformance.

  8. Patient case explorer.

  9. Data quality and methodology notes.

Use a collapsible sidebar with navigation links:

  • Overview

  • Process Flow

  • Activity Analysis

  • Duration Analysis

  • Bottlenecks

  • Conformance

  • Case Explorer

  • Data Quality

14. Final quality expectations

The final dashboard must be:

  • Fully responsive.

  • Visually polished and professional.

  • Interactive, not just a static mockup.

  • Easy for beginners and evaluators to understand.

  • Consistent in colors, spacing, typography, and chart styling.

  • Built with reusable components and clean code.

  • Equipped with meaningful empty states and error messages.

  • Designed for clear analytical storytelling.

Add a short footer:

“CareFlow – Clinical Pathway Process Mining | Healthcare Workflow Analytics | Academic Project using Synthetic EHR Data”

Most important instruction: Prioritize analytical accuracy over visual decoration. Never invent patient statistics, process transitions, waiting times, efficiency improvements, or conformance scores. If a metric cannot be calculated from the available dataset, show “Not available” rather than displaying a fabricated value.

Recommended dashboard appearance

Healthcare analytics overview
Patient journey process map
Activity and duration analysis
Patient case explorer

My recommendation: Upload careflow_cleaned_event_logs.csv along with this prompt when using the dashboard generator. That way, it can calculate the charts and KPIs from your actual project data instead of creating a dashboard filled with made-up numbers.

One important point for your project evaluation: show PM4Py process discovery and conformance results as pending until those analyses have actually been executed.

CareFlow – Project Progress Report (Work Completed So Far)

So far, we have made good progress on our CareFlow – Clinical Pathway Process Mining project. We started by understanding the project requirements and setting up the basic project structure. We then created a synthetic healthcare event-log dataset containing 500 patient cases and 3,472 recorded events.

We cleaned and prepared the dataset by standardizing column names, checking timestamps, sorting events chronologically, and checking for duplicate or missing records. We also analyzed repeated activities and found that 442 cases contained repeated activities, including 126 cases with repeated triage.

After preparing the data, we created an initial process-flow visualization to get a better understanding of how patients move through different hospital activities. We also prepared Python scripts for process discovery and PM4Py event-log loading, along with an XES event-log file for further process mining analysis.

On the technical side, we prepared the initial dbt models and BigQuery setup files to support future data transformation and analysis. We also planned the dashboard structure, including patient journey flow, activity analysis, journey duration, potential bottlenecks, and key performance indicators.

At present, our main progress includes:

  • Project structure and requirements setup.

  • Synthetic healthcare dataset generation.

  • Data cleaning and preprocessing.

  • Data quality checks and reporting.

  • Initial process-flow visualization.

  • PM4Py loading script and XES file preparation.

  • Initial dbt models and BigQuery configuration files.

  • Dashboard planning and KPI identification.

Work still in progress: Actual PM4Py execution and process discovery, conformance checking, BigQuery/dbt execution, SQL-based KPI calculations, and final dashboard integration.

Overall, we have completed the initial data preparation and project setup stages. We now have a prepared dataset and the basic tools needed to move towards deeper process analysis and dashboard development.

4. Short report for your project documentation

We analyzed the cleaned healthcare event log to discover the patient journey process model. The analysis covered 500 patient cases and 3,472 recorded events across seven clinical activities. The results show that most patient journeys begin with registration, followed by triage and doctor consultation. Some patients then undergo laboratory tests or X-rays before returning to consultation and proceeding to treatment and discharge. We also identified repeated triage and consultation activities, highlighting workflow patterns that can be investigated further. These repetitions do not automatically indicate inefficiency and require additional analysis.

Technical note: This is a directly-follows process model calculated from the cleaned dataset. PM4Py was not installed in this environment, so the PM4Py discovery API has not yet been executed. The generated model is a useful initial process discovery result, but should not yet be described as PM4Py-validated.
